name: Meningitis
tagline: Stiff neck, severe headache, purple rash.

urgent.heading: Urgent — go to hospital now
urgent.primary_message: Bacterial meningitis can kill within hours. Do not wait for all symptoms — get to hospital immediately.
red_flags: A purple-red rash that does NOT fade when pressed under a glass
Stiff neck — cannot touch chin to chest
Severe headache with fever and vomiting
Sensitivity to light, sounds, or touch
Seizures or a high-pitched cry in a baby
Bulging soft spot on a baby's head, with fever and refusal to feed

what_is_it.heading: Meningitis in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Meningitis is an infection of the meninges — the protective layers around the brain and spinal cord. Bacterial meningitis is one of the fastest-killing infections known.
paragraphs: Most meningitis is caused by either a virus or a bacteria. Viral meningitis is usually milder and gets better on its own. Bacterial meningitis is a true emergency — it can kill a healthy person within hours and needs antibiotics fast.

From the outside, you cannot reliably tell the two apart. That is why every suspected case must be treated as bacterial until proven otherwise. South Africa runs vaccination programmes against the most dangerous strains.

items.headline: Kills in hours
items.body: Bacterial meningitis can go from first symptom to death in under 24 hours. Speed of treatment is everything.

items.headline: Vaccine-preventable
items.body: Free SA childhood vaccines (Hib, Pneumococcal, Meningococcal) prevent the most dangerous strains. Get them on time.

items.headline: Close contact risk
items.body: Spreads through coughing, sneezing, kissing, or sharing drinks. Close contacts may be given antibiotics as a precaution.

items.headline: Tumbler test
items.body: Press a clear glass against the rash. If the spots do not fade under pressure — go straight to hospital.

pull_quote.text: Trust your instinct. If something feels seriously wrong — especially in a child — do not wait for the full set of symptoms. Go to hospital. Meningitis can kill before all signs appear.

signs.heading: What to watch for
signs.lede: Symptoms can start like flu, then worsen fast. The classic signs may not appear in the same order — or at all in babies and young children.

items.title: Adults & older children
items.description: High fever, severe headache, stiff neck (cannot touch chin to chest), light sensitivity, nausea or vomiting, confusion or drowsiness.

items.title: The purple rash
items.description: Small reddish-purple spots or blotches that look like bruises. Spreads rapidly. Does not fade when pressed with a glass — this is an emergency.

items.title: Babies and toddlers
items.description: High-pitched moaning cry, refusing feeds, very floppy or very stiff, bulging soft spot, blotchy or pale skin, fever with cold hands and feet.

items.title: Cold extremities first
items.description: Hands and feet going cold while the body is hot, severe leg pain, and unusually pale skin can be earlier signs than the rash or stiff neck.

spreads.heading: How meningitis spreads
yes: Coughing and sneezing from someone carrying the bacteria
Sharing cups, water bottles, cigarettes, or cutlery
Living in close quarters — university residences, military barracks, prisons
no: Casual contact like handshakes or being in the same room
Toilet seats, swimming pools, or door handles

prevention.heading: How to protect yourself and your family
prevention.lede: Vaccines protect against the most dangerous types of bacterial meningitis. They are free at every SA government clinic for children, and recommended for higher-risk adults.

items.title: Free childhood vaccines
items.description: Hib at 6, 10, 14 weeks. Pneumococcal at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, 9 months. Meningococcal where indicated. Follow the SA schedule.

items.title: Higher-risk groups
items.description: University students in residences, military recruits, travellers to the African meningitis belt or Hajj — ask your doctor about Meningococcal ACWY vaccine.

items.title: If a close contact is sick
items.description: Household members and close contacts of a bacterial meningitis case are usually offered preventive antibiotics by Public Health. Take them — they work.

items.title: Recognise early — act fast
items.description: Knowing the symptoms saves lives. Trust your instinct. If something is seriously wrong, get to hospital.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Only babies and children get meningitis.
items.fact: Babies, teenagers, and young adults are at higher risk, but it can strike at any age. Teenage and university residence outbreaks are common.

items.myth: If the rash still fades when I press it, it isn't meningitis.
items.fact: Early in meningitis the rash can still fade. If other symptoms are present — headache, fever, neck stiffness — go to hospital regardless.

items.myth: Early antibiotics at the clinic are enough.
items.fact: Bacterial meningitis needs intravenous antibiotics in hospital, plus monitoring. Tablet antibiotics alone are not enough.
Vaccines protect against the most common bacterial causes. They do not cause the disease. The childhood schedule's vaccines are safe and life-saving.

action_steps.heading: What to do — the moment you suspect meningitis

items.title: Do the tumbler test
items.description: Press the side of a clear glass firmly against the rash. If the spots stay visible through the glass — go to hospital now.

items.title: Call 10177 or go straight to the emergency room
items.description: Say 'suspected meningitis' at triage so you are seen immediately. Do not wait for a GP appointment.

items.title: Note when symptoms started
items.description: Time matters. Tell the hospital team when the fever, headache, rash, or behaviour change began.

items.title: Do not wait for all symptoms
items.description: The classic triad of fever, stiff neck, and headache may never all appear together. Each one alone is a reason to be checked.

items.title: Tell close contacts
items.description: Anyone who has shared a household, cup, or kiss in the last week must contact Public Health for advice. Antibiotic prophylaxis may be offered.

get_help.heading: Who to call right now
get_help.lede: Suspected bacterial meningitis is one of the few illnesses where 'go to hospital now' is the right answer — even at 3am, even if you are not sure.
